newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-German chemicals industry upbeat for 1997.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-German chemicals industry upbeat for 1997.

text.p: Germany's chemical industry is upbeat for 1997 as a whole after reporting a strong start to the year, fuelled both by revived global economic growth and more favourable exchange rates.

"Recovery in the German chemical industry has continued at the start of 1997," Utz-Hellmuth Felcht, a board member at Germany's Hoechst AG and head of Dechema, a German scientific technical society, told reporters at a news conference .

"Key elements for ongoing, positive developments are more favourable now than they have been for a long time, considering currency relationships, low interest rates and moderate wage agreements," Felcht said.
Earlier, the VCI chemical industry association said industry production had expanded by an average 7.5 percent in both January and February, indicating last year's recovery was now picking up steam.

While the Germany chemical industry roared out of recession to a string of record results in early 1995, sluggish global economic growth and collapsing prices in some sectors braked developments, leading to more moderate growth early last year.

Now reaping the benefits of a weaker mark which makes German goods abroad less expensive and underpins the export- driven industry, the chemical sector is betting on improved conditions in the coming months.

"The majority of chemical groups is expecting a firming of the positive signals in the coming months," VCI said in a statement, adding that these expecations were based largely on a booming export business.
The mark hit an all-time high against the dollar in the Spring of 1995, severely denting the results at Germany's three biggest chemical and drugs groups Hoechst AG, Bayer AG and BASF AG.
Felcht said that in view of higher anticipated foreign growth rates and increasing industry globalisation, German companies would likely need to make more investments abroad.
"All big investments in the chemical industry are currently being made in southeast Asia."

Turning to western Europe, where Dechema does expect higher growth rates this year, Felcht said impulses would need to be generated through new innovations and by producing products that need to be made close to the markets where they are consumed.

Dampening the industry's generally upbeat mood slightly might be expectations that domestic demand will remain sluggish especially in view of Germany's stubbornly high unemployment rate and an anticipated increase in social costs, the VCI said.
While industry production picked up markedly during the first two months of the year, the VCI said that developments in turnover, like last year, were split in early 1997.

For the full year 1996, German domestic chemical groups had turnover of 175.5 billion marks ($102.9 billion) but a clear drop in chemical producer prices cut into sales. "The lower sales are exclusively related to domestic business," the VCI said.

Last year's producer prices in the chemical industry were 3.6 percent below 1995 levels and while there was a slight stabilisation in prices at the beginning of 1997, the VCI said "a lasting change in the trend is still not visible."
VCI said the chemical industry was able to fulfil last year's wage contract requirement to secure trainee positions within the industry.

On the other hand, Felcht stressed that the industry was not able to employ all chemists holding doctorate degrees, noting that in past years universities had produced a surplus of graduates in chemistry.

"It is impossible (to employ all chemists who have earned doctorate degrees)" Felcht said, urging graduates to consider jobs in related industries or moves into industries like banking or insurance, where technical qualifications are needed. Currently some 4,000 chemists holding doctorate degrees are unemployed in Germany.
